title: DOJ Sues Arizona and Three States Over In-State Tuition for Undocumented Dreamers
excerpt: The Justice Department has now filed 21 lawsuits challenging state laws that allow undocumented students to pay in-state college tuition, targeting Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington in its latest action.
body:
• The DOJ filed lawsuits against Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington, challenging state laws that provide in-state tuition to undocumented students, bringing total suits to 21 states.
  • In Arizona, the lawsuit targets voter-approved Proposition 308, which allows undocumented high school graduates to pay in-state tuition. The DOJ estimates 3,600 students per year could qualify.
  • At Arizona State University alone, undocumented students received an estimated $10.5 million in reduced tuition based on the roughly $24,000 difference between in-state and out-of-state rates.
  • Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes, who previously defended the law, is reviewing the lawsuit. Advocacy groups say the suit contradicts the will of Arizona voters who approved the measure in 2022.

The U.S. Department of Justice has escalated its campaign against in-state tuition benefits for undocumented immigrants, filing lawsuits against Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington on August 27 — the latest in a sweeping effort that has now targeted 21 states.

The complaints seek to block enforcement of state laws that allow undocumented residents who attended and graduated from local high schools to pay in-state tuition rates at public colleges and universities. The DOJ argues these laws discriminate against U.S. citizens from other states who are not eligible for the same reduced rates.

Arizona at the Center

The Arizona lawsuit has drawn particular attention because it targets Proposition 308, a ballot measure approved by 51% of Arizona voters in 2022. The law allows undocumented students who attended and graduated from Arizona high schools to pay in-state tuition rather than significantly higher out-of-state rates.

https://x.com/MichaelARothman/status/2093865201435300093

According to the DOJ complaint, more than 3,600 undocumented immigrants per year could qualify for in-state tuition under Arizona's law, citing figures from the Arizona Center for Investigative Reporting. In the fall 2025 semester, at least 720 undocumented students received in-state tuition, including 432 at Arizona State University.

Given the roughly $24,000 difference between in-state and out-of-state tuition at ASU, the DOJ estimates undocumented students received approximately $10.5 million in reduced tuition at that institution alone.

"Over 30 years ago, Congress made clear that states cannot put illegal aliens before our nation's own citizens."

— Stanley E. Woodward Jr., Associate Attorney General

Five States Already Blocked

The latest filings bring the DOJ's total to 21 lawsuits against states challenging in-state tuition for undocumented students. Under Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, the department has already secured favorable rulings in five states — Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, and Illinois — where courts permanently enjoined similar laws, including a decision from the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=vHrdkkPFuMA

Additional suits are pending in 12 more states including California, New York, Virginia, New Jersey, Colorado, Minnesota, Massachusetts, Maryland, Kansas, Rhode Island, Connecticut, and Vermont.

Arizona Pushes Back

Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes, a Democrat, is reviewing the DOJ lawsuit, according to spokesperson Richie Taylor. Mayes issued a legal opinion last year defending the law, arguing it is tied to high school attendance and graduation rather than residency status, and therefore does not violate federal law.

The Arizona Latino Legislative Caucus condemned the lawsuit, arguing that students who attended Arizona schools and graduated from Arizona high schools are making contributions to the state's economy.

"I have no doubt that the DOJ will lose this battle in the courts."

— Reyna Montoya, Founder and CEO of Aliento

Montoya, whose organization supports Dreamers and mixed-status families, said the lawsuit is sowing confusion among undocumented students who remain legally eligible for in-state tuition while the case is litigated.

Impact on Indian Diaspora Students

While the majority of Dreamer students affected by in-state tuition laws are of Latin American origin, Indian nationals represent a growing share of undocumented immigrants in the United States. Indians have been among the fastest-growing groups of undocumented border crossers in recent years, and many brought children who now face the same educational access questions.

For Indian-American families in mixed-status households — including those with children who aged out of dependent visa status or whose parents' immigration cases are pending — the in-state tuition question is directly relevant. The outcome of these lawsuits could determine whether their children can afford college in the states where they grew up.

What's Next

The lawsuits are part of the Trump administration's broader effort to restrict benefits for undocumented immigrants. While the DOJ has secured injunctions in five states, the outcomes in Arizona and other states with voter-approved measures remain uncertain. Courts will weigh whether federal law preempts state tuition policies or whether states retain authority to set their own eligibility criteria for public education benefits.
